title_eng: An Investigation of the Effect of Sampling Frequency to the Frequency Domain Analysis of Pulse Rate Variability
title_kor: An Investigation of the Effect of Sampling Frequency to the Frequency Domain Analysis of Pulse Rate Variability
abstract:
Abstract—This study aims to investigate the effect of 
sampling frequency to the frequency domain analysis of pulse 
rate variability. Six frequency domain variables (VLF, LF, HF, 
LF/HF, nLF and nHF) were derived from five down-sampled 
signals (100 Hz, 50 Hz, 25 Hz, 10 Hz and 5 Hz ) and compared 
with reference result derived from 10 kHz -sampled ECG. As a 
result, it was found that HF, LF/HF , nLF and nHF have 
significant difference (p<0.05) at < 10 Hz sampling rate . 
Moreover, at 5 Hz sampling rate, every variable except VLF and 
LF showed the significant difference. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Pulse rate variability (PRV) is regarded as an alternative of 
HRV in many research [1]. In most cases, the PRV is derived 
from photo-plethysmography (PPG) because the PPG system 
is non-invasive, cheap and easy to implement. However, 
optical sensor typically needs high power consumption, thus 
optimizing sampling frequency (fs) of PPG system is quite 
important to extend the battery life as well as to improve the 
accuracy of the analysis. In this research, we investigated the 
effect of sampling frequency to the frequency domain analysis 
of PRV derived from down -sampled PPG and validated the 
result compare d with HRV derive d from high 
frequency-sampled ECG. 
II. MATERIALS AND METHOD 
Electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmogram 
(PPG) were simultaneously recorded at 10 kHz sampling 
frequency with 20-minute length. Twenty -eight healthy 
volunteers were participated in the experiment, and every 
subject was asked to relax during data acquisition in supine 
position. We decimated the 10 kHz-sampled PPG by 100, 200, 
400, 1,000 and 2,000 to generate 100, 50, 25, 10 and 5 
Hz-sampled signal, respectively. PRV was analyzed with 
systolic peaks of PPG waveform. Before analyzing the PRV, 
every peak location was detected and validated by p roficient 
researchers. Typical frequency domain variables -VLF, LF, 
HF, LF/HF, nLF and nHF [2] - were derived from signals at 
each sampling frequency and compared with the result of 
HRV analysis based on 10 kHz-sampled ECG.

result, it was found that HF, LF/HF , nLF and nHF have 
significant difference (p<0.05) at < 10 Hz sampling rate . 
Moreover, at 5 Hz sampling rate, every variable except VLF and 
LF showed the significant difference. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Pulse rate variability (PRV) is regarded as an alternative of 
HRV in many research [1]. In most cases, the PRV is derived 
from photo-plethysmography (PPG) because the PPG system 
is non-invasive, cheap and easy to implement. However, 
optical sensor typically needs high power consumption, thus 
optimizing sampling frequency (fs) of PPG system is quite 
important to extend the battery life as well as to improve the 
accuracy of the analysis. In this research, we investigated the 
effect of sampling frequency to the frequency domain analysis 
of PRV derived from down -sampled PPG and validated the 
result compare d with HRV derive d from high 
frequency-sampled ECG. 
II. MATERIALS AND METHOD 
Electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmogram 
(PPG) were simultaneously recorded at 10 kHz sampling 
frequency with 20-minute length. Twenty -eight healthy 
volunteers were participated in the experiment, and every 
subject was asked to relax during data acquisition in supine 
position. We decimated the 10 kHz-sampled PPG by 100, 200, 
400, 1,000 and 2,000 to generate 100, 50, 25, 10 and 5 
Hz-sampled signal, respectively. PRV was analyzed with 
systolic peaks of PPG waveform. Before analyzing the PRV, 
every peak location was detected and validated by p roficient 
researchers. Typical frequency domain variables -VLF, LF, 
HF, LF/HF, nLF and nHF [2] - were derived from signals at 
each sampling frequency and compared with the result of 
HRV analysis based on 10 kHz-sampled ECG. 
III. RESULT AND DISCUSSION 
Fig. 1 shows that the fractional change of frequency 
domain variables of PRV according to the sampling 
frequency. In statistical validation, one -way ANOV A 
indicates a difference in HF, LF/HF, nLF and nHF with 
p<0.05 and the Bonferroni post-hoc test indicated a 
significance difference ( p<0.05) between frequency groups; 
nHF is significantly different at fs =10 Hz; HF, LF/HF, nLF 
and nHF are significantly different at fs = 5 Hz ; significant 
difference was not found in every variable at fs ≥ 25 Hz. This 
result could be interpreted that there are no differences of 
frequency domain analysis between reference HRV and PRV 
when PPG’s sampling frequency is over 25 Hz. However, at fs 
≤ 10 Hz, significant differences were found in some variables. 
Especially, significant differences were dramatically 
increased at fs ≤ 10 Hz, and it could be postulated that this 
phenomenon comes from the spectral characteristic of PPG; 
power spectrum of PPG consists of the fundamental frequency 
around heart rate which has most of energy and its harmonics. 
Assuming the heart rate is 70 bpm (1.2 Hz), 10 Hz sampling 
frequency could cause aliasing of 4th (6.0 Hz) or higher order 
of harmonic components by Shannon’s sampling theorem. 
IV. CONCLUSION 
In this research, we showed that fs ≤ 10 Hz could cause 
erroneous results of frequency domain analysis of PRV. To 
suggest more delicate result, further studies should be carried 
out with various sampling frequencies between 10 to 25 Hz. 
REFERENCES 
[1] A. Schafer and J. Vagedes, "How accurate is pulse rate variability as an 
estimate of heart rate variability? A review on studies comparing 
photoplethysmographic technology with an electrocardiogram," 
International Journal of Cardiology, vol. 166, pp. 15-29, Jun 5 2013. 
[2] Task Force of th e European Society of Cardiology, "Heart rate 
variability standards of measurement, physiological interpretation, and 
clinical use," Eur Heart J, vol. 17, pp. 354-381, 1996.
